title: Decision trees
summary: A decision tree asks a sequence of yes/no questions, each comparing one feature with a threshold, so it cuts the feature space into axis-aligned rectangles. Each cut is chosen greedily to reduce Gini impurity the most. Unlimited depth memorises the data; depth limits, minimum leaf sizes and pruning regularise it, and ensembles (random forests, gradient boosting) make trees strong and stable.
llm_link: Language models do not use decision trees, but mixture-of-experts models contain a learned router that sends each token to a few of many expert sub-networks: a soft, trainable cousin of a tree's branching question.
key_ideas: Each internal node asks 'is feature f < t?'. Geometrically that is a straight cut parallel to an axis, and the leaves are rectangles.
Gini impurity G = 1 − Σ pₖ²: 0 for a pure group, 0.5 for a 50/50 mix of two classes.
A split is scored by the size-weighted average impurity of its two sides; the tree keeps the split that lowers impurity most.
Trees are grown greedily and recursively until a stopping rule (pure, too few points, depth limit).
Deep trees overfit. Random forests average many trees trained on resampled data; gradient boosting adds trees that correct the remaining errors.

quiz.q: A node holds 10 points: 7 of class A and 3 of class B. What is its Gini impurity?
Predict the result: a split sends 4 points (all class A) left and 4 points (2 A, 2 B) right. What is the weighted Gini of the split?
quiz.explain: Left is pure (G = 0). Right is 50/50 (G = 0.5). Weighted: (4·0 + 4·0.5) / 8 = 0.25.

quiz.q: What shape are the regions a decision tree carves out of a 2-feature plane?
options: Rectangles with sides parallel to the axes
quiz.explain: Each question compares one feature with a number, which is a vertical or horizontal cut. Combining them gives axis-aligned rectangles.

quiz.q: Why does a random forest usually beat a single deep tree on new data?
options: Each tree in it is deeper
Averaging many trees trained on different resamples cancels out their individual quirks, lowering variance
It trains on the test set
quiz.explain: A single tree is unstable: small data changes can change its first question. Averaging many decorrelated trees keeps their shared signal and cancels the noise.

quiz.q: In a mixture-of-experts language model, what does the router do?
options: Sends each token to a few of many expert sub-networks, a learned and soft version of a branching question
Builds a decision tree over the vocabulary
quiz.explain: Only the selected experts process the token, so the model can have many parameters while using a fraction of them per token. The router is trained along with everything else.

problems.title: Gini impurity
problems.prompt:
Write gini(labels) for a plain list of labels (any hashable values): 1 minus the sum, over classes, of the squared fraction of labels in that class. An empty list has impurity 0.

gini(['a', 'a', 'a'])        # 0.0
gini(['a', 'b'])             # 0.5
gini(['a'] * 7 + ['b'] * 3)  # 0.42
problems.starter:
def gini(labels):
    n = len(labels)
    if n == 0:
        return 0.0
    # TODO 1: count how many times each label appears (a dict works)
    # TODO 2: return 1 - sum of (count / n) ** 2
    pass

tests.name: pure group
tests.code:
out = gini(['a', 'a', 'a'])
assert out is not None, 'gini returned None'
assert abs(out) < 1e-12, f'a pure group has impurity 0, got {out}'

tests.name: fifty-fifty
tests.code:
out = gini(['a', 'b', 'a', 'b'])
assert abs(out - 0.5) < 1e-12, f'a 50/50 mix of two classes has impurity 0.5, got {out}'

tests.name: three classes
tests.code:
out = gini([0, 1, 2])
assert abs(out - 2/3) < 1e-12, f'three equal classes: 1 - 3*(1/3)**2 = 2/3, got {out}'

hints:
counts = {}
for y in labels: counts[y] = counts.get(y, 0) + 1
return 1 - sum((c / n) ** 2 for c in counts.values())

problems.title: The best threshold for one feature
problems.prompt:
Write best_split(xs, ys): try every threshold halfway between two neighbouring distinct values of xs; for each one, send points with x < t left and the rest right, and compute the weighted impurity

(len(left) · gini(left) + len(right) · gini(right)) / n

Return (best_t, best_score) for the lowest score. A gini function is provided.

best_split([1, 2, 3, 10, 11, 12], ['a','a','a','b','b','b'])  # (6.5, 0.0)

tests.name: perfect split
tests.code:
t, s = best_split([1, 2, 3, 10, 11, 12], ['a', 'a', 'a', 'b', 'b', 'b'])
assert t == 6.5 and abs(s) < 1e-12, f'the gap between 3 and 10 separates the classes perfectly: expected (6.5, 0.0), got ({t}, {s})'

tests.name: order of input does not matter
tests.code:
t, s = best_split([12, 1, 11, 2, 10, 3], ['b', 'a', 'b', 'a', 'b', 'a'])
assert t == 6.5, f'pair each x with its own label (zip), then threshold on x: expected 6.5, got {t}'

tests.name: weighted by size
tests.code:
t, s = best_split([1, 2, 3, 4], ['a', 'a', 'b', 'a'])
assert t == 2.5 and abs(s - 0.25) < 1e-9, f'cut at 2.5: left [a, a] is pure, right [b, a] has gini 0.5, weighted (2*0 + 2*0.5)/4 = 0.25. Got ({t}, {s}); weight each side by its size'

tests.name: no split possible
tests.code:
t, s = best_split([5, 5, 5], ['a', 'b', 'a'])
assert t is None, 'with only one distinct x value there is nothing to split on: return (None, inf)'

hints: left = [y for x, y in zip(xs, ys) if x < t]; right = [y for x, y in zip(xs, ys) if x >= t]
if score < best_score: best_t, best_score = t, score

problems.title: Walk down a tree
problems.prompt:
A tree is stored as nested dicts. An internal node looks like {'feature': 0, 'threshold': 2.5, 'left': ..., 'right': ...} and a leaf looks like {'label': 'cat'}. Go left when x[feature] < threshold, otherwise right.

Write predict(tree, x) that returns the leaf's label, using a while loop (no recursion needed).
problems.starter:
tree = {'feature': 0, 'threshold': 50,
        'left': {'label': 'decline'},
        'right': {'feature': 1, 'threshold': 40,
                  'left': {'label': 'approve'},
                  'right': {'label': 'review'}}}

def predict(tree, x):
    node = tree
    # TODO: while the node is not a leaf, step left or right
    return None

tests.name: left leaf
tests.code: assert predict(tree, [30, 25]) == 'decline', 'x[0] = 30 < 50 goes left to decline'

tests.name: two steps
tests.code:
assert predict(tree, [80, 25]) == 'approve', 'x[0] = 80 goes right, then x[1] = 25 < 40 goes left to approve'
assert predict(tree, [80, 60]) == 'review', 'x[0] = 80 right, x[1] = 60 right: review'

tests.name: threshold itself goes right
tests.code: assert predict(tree, [50, 0]) == 'approve', 'x < threshold goes left, so x == threshold goes right'

tests.name: a single leaf is a tree too
tests.code: assert predict({'label': 'only'}, [1, 2]) == 'only', 'a tree that is just a leaf always predicts its label'

hints: node = node['left'] if x[node['feature']] < node['threshold'] else node['right']
